title.narrative: UNODC Anti-Corruption: Citizen-focused Accountability and Transparency in ASEAN
UNODC Anti-Corruption: Citizen-focused Accountability and Transparency in ASEAN

description.narrative:
As highlighted in the Strategy for Sweden’s regional development cooperation with Asia and the Pacific Region in 2022–2026, democratic development and respect for human rights and the rule of law have regressed in a number of cases. Space for the media and civil society to operate freely has shrunken markedly. In addition, corruption is widespread.
An integrated approach within and between the areas of the strategy is sought in the project, primarily through UNODC's choice of partners, were several also are involved in the environment and climate efforts in the region. The project thus works to prevent and fight corruption when it comes to crimes that affect the environment. One of the long term missions of UNODC is to help make the world safer from corruption. This would also reduce the exposure for people living in poverty and vulnerable situations, when it comes to extreme climate-related events and other shocks in society.
During the operationalisation process of the new swedish strategi, the embassy identified a gap regarding a direct anti-corruption support. Looking at indirect support and integration of anti-corruption, there are several examples in the current portfolio. Given limitations in the budget for 2023, the size of the project has decreased, and the geographical scope is set to be ASEAN subregion.
Legal frameworks: The UN Convention Against Corruption (UNCAC) is the first and unique global legally binding anti-corruption instrument. It introduces a comprehensive set of standards, measures and rules to fight corruption. UNCAC provides a comprehensive framework to strengthen anti-corruption programmes in the region. Following the Convention's provisions, all countries in the region need to undergo a review of compliance. The review process comprises two five-year cycles.
Corruption and poverty: As stated in the Regional Multi-Dimensional Poverty Analysis (MDPA) conducted by Sida, the lack of strong and independent democratic institutions and limits to a free press has made corruption widespread. Grand corruption by elites in the private sector, the government and the military is a major problem in the region, this high-level abuse of power that favors the few at the expense of the many can destroy entire sectors, create recessions and stop democracies. Through its work at global, regional and national levels on Alternative Development and on Corruption, UNODC provides support to Member States to reach their Targets under the various SDGs, including SDG 1 on ending poverty and the related targets 1.4, on equal rights to economic resources, and 1.5, on building the resilience of the poor and those in vulnerable situations. Corruption hurts the poor disproportionately by diverting funds intended for development, undermining a Government’s ability to provide basic services, feeding inequality and injustice and discouraging foreign aid and investment. Corruption is a key element in economic underperformance and a major obstacle to poverty alleviation and development.
Through the framework of the UN Convention Against Corruption (UNCAC), UNODC provides support to Member States in developing national and regional capacities to prevent and effectively address corruption and its links with poverty. The initiatives supported by UNODC aim at strengthening anti-corruption policies, legislation and strategies, enhancing regional anti-corruption networks and institutions, and promoting anti-corruption strategies with the private sector, civil society and academia thus accelerating progress towards sustainable development and poverty reduction.

Som angivet i Strategi för Sveriges regionala utvecklingssamarbete med Asien och Oceanien 2022-2026 så har den demokratiska utvecklingen, respekten för mänskliga rättigheter och rättsstatens principer på flera håll gått bakåt. Utrymmet för media och civilsamhälle att fritt verka har minskat påtagligt och korruptionen är utbredd.
En integrerad ansats inom och mellan strategins områden eftersträvas i insatsen, främst genom UNODCs val av partners, vilket innefattar aktörer verksamma inom miljö-och klimatområdet. Projektet verkar därmed för att förebygga och bekämpa korruption när det gäller brott som påvekar miljön. En minskad korruption, som är en långsiktig vision för UNODC, minskar också den utsatthet och sårbarhet som människor som lever i fattigdom utsätts för gällande extrema klimatrelaterade händelser och andra chocker i samhällen.
Under operationaliseringsprocessen har ambassaden identifierat ett gap i nuvarande portfölj när det gäller ett direkt antikorruptionsstöd. Gällande indirekt stöd och integration av antikorruption finns flera exempel i portföljen. Givet nedskärningar i budget har storleken på projektet minskat, och det geografiska fokuset är på subregionen ASEAN.
Internationella ramverk: FN:s konvention mot korruption (UNCAC) är det första, unika globala antikorruptionsinstrument som är rättsligt bindande. UNCAC innefattar en omfattande uppsättning av standarder, åtgärder och regler för att bekämpa korruption. UNCAC tillhandahåller ett ramverk för att stärka anti-korruptionsprogram i regionen. Enligt konventionens bestämmelser måste alla länder i regionen genomgå en granskning av efterlevnaden. Översynsprocessen omfattar två femårscykler.
Korruption och fattigdom: I Sidas regionala Multidimensionella Fattigdomsanalys (MDPA) anges att bristen på effektiva och oberoende demokratiska institutioner och begränsningar för en den fria pressen att verka, har gjort att korruptionen utbredd. Korrupta eliter inom den privata sektorn, och/eller regeringar och militär, är ett stort problem i regionen. Denna typ av maktmissbruk på hög nivå gynnar de få på, bekostnad av många, ochpåverkar mycket negativt flera sektorer, bidrar till lågkonjunkturer och hindrar demokratisk utveckling. Genom sitt arbete på global, regional och nationell nivå, med fokus på Alternativ utveckling och korruption, ger UNODC stöd till medlemsstaterna i att nå sina mål under de olika SDG, inklusive SDG 1, Ingen fattigdom, och de relaterade delmålen 1.4, Lika rätt till egendom, grundläggande tjänster, teknologi och ekonomiska resurser och 1,5, Bygg motståndskraft mot ekonomiska, sociala och miljömässiga katastrofer. Korruption skadar människor som lever i fattigdom oproportionerligt genom att finansiella medel avsedda för utveckling avleds. Korruption avskräcker internationella investeringar och undergräver regeringars förmåga att tillhandahålla grundläggande tjänster, vilket ökar ojämlikhet och orättvisor i samhället. Korruption är därmed ett stort hinder för fattigdomsbekämpning och utveckling.
Inom ramen för UNCAC ger UNODC stöd till medlemsstaterna i att utveckla nationell och regional kapacitet för att förebygga och effektivt ta itu med korruption och dess kopplingar till fattigdom. Initiativ som stöds av UNODC syftar till att stärka antikorruptionspolitik, lagstiftning och strategier, stärka regionala antikorruptionsnätverk och institutioner, och främja anti-korruptionsstrategier med den privata sektorn, civilsamhället och akademin och på så sätt påskynda framstegen mot hållbar utveckling och fattigdomsbekämpning.

The overall results of this intervention achieved in 2025 are that Swedens support has enabled UNODC to help moving from initial pilot with the SEA-ACN and JAC anti-corruption efforts into action networks, beyond capacity building to advance their advocacy and corruption reporting. From the initial pilot initiative of testing whether anti-corruption engagement with non-state actors could be strengthened through a regional platform approach, the intervention has proved that strong demand and demonstrated impact for the need of non-state actors to engage in anti-corruption and with government authorities has led to the expansion of the initiative into a broader regional platform which is beneficial to anti-corruption reform and efforts at country level.
From the highlighted activities implemented in 2025, several results and impacts are shown:
- Joint anti-corruption efforts were enhanced between the SEA-ACN and JAC networks.
Joint workshops have enabled members of the two anti-corruption networks deepen their collaboration through jointly designed areas and methods to advance corruption investigation, notably in public procurement, open data for corruption investigation, beneficial ownership transparency. Enhanced capacity of the two networks and their ongoing activities through the support and expertise facilitation of UNODC has enabled them to more effectively engage in anti-corruption advocacy, reporting and policy reforms in dialogue and policy action with government and oversight bodies. Their enhanced capacity enables their effective participation in holding governments accountable and anti-corruption reforms in the region. - Key results from the SEA-ACN and JAC networks substantive collaboration are derived from the focus on procurement integrity and data-driven accountability has helped to foster new connections between civil society actors and media professionals across Southeast Asia. Their established Open Data Platform has been a direct result of the demand for information and open data to enable their investigation linked to PEPs and beneficial ownership, which were done as a joint agenda to design capacity training and innovate working methods. Together, their joint work has fostered cross-sectoral learning, built investigative capacity, and laid out the groundwork for sustained collaboration on public procurement reform, open data, and anti-corruption advocacy. It also resulted in support to how journalists can use open data to investigate PEPs and uncover corruption networks, reinforcing the role of media in promoting transparency and accountability.
- JAC and the model for cross-border collaboration of investigative journalism
Funding from Sweden has enabled the JAC to launch regional calls for proposals to fund investigative journalism on corruption issues. These grants enabled the publication of impactful investigations that have advanced public awareness and accountability in corruption-related cases. The five investigative journalism grants in 2025 were: • IndonesiaCambodia: Cambodian Gambling Tentacles (Tempo Magazine, April 2025) exposed Indonesian business links to Cambodias gambling and scam industries, revealing political and financial networks behind the illicit trade. The story generated significant public engagement and online debate. • The Philippines: Rappler published multiple stories (MarchAugust 2025) revealing conflicts of interest and corruption in public infrastructure contracts involving members of Congress. These investigations spurred national discussion and contributed to an upcoming parliamentary inquiry on public works contracting. • IndonesiaCambodia: Nasari TVs June 2025 documentary Tracing the Death of Soleh uncovered a human trafficking case linked to fraudulent job offers. The investigation prompted Indonesian authorities to pursue suspects and assist victims, and reached over 500,000 viewers online. • Philippines: GMA News Online reported on the resurgence of criminal online scam networks following official bans, including coverage of their cross-border operations and alleged links to corrupt officials. • ThailandCambodia: An experimental grant supported journalist and influencer Patpon Artie Sabpaitoon to conduct investigative work on corruption-related risks at the ThailandCambodia border.
The impacts and results from these investigative journalism grants have been highlighted in earlier result reporting to Sida in anti-corruption contribution, particularly from the investigation and reporting on corruption in governments public infrastructure projects involving members of the Congress in the Philippines. The Sida grant for investigative journalism to the Rappler journalist has spurred national outrage and demand for the ongoing parliamentary inquiry commissioned by the President. Global visibility and effort to prioritize anti-corruption in media reporting by the JAC model of cross-border investigative journalist collaboration has been recognized and shared to international anti-corruption audience.
- Effective non-state actor engagement with government authorities on anti-corruption policy and reforms
Several results are shown from increased non-state actor engagement with government authorities in anti-corruption across the region and at country level in 2025. For example: • How civil society shaped freedom of information (FOI) reform in the Philippines The recent landmark adoption of the FOI bill in the Philippines, which had remained pending for nearly four decades, is evidence of strong anti-corruption and transparency CSO engagement. They have played a key role in driving public demand for and sustaining reform momentum to influence oversight bodies to enact. • Engaging non-state actors in anti-corruption in Vietnam Convened by UNODC, non-state actors together with business associations, and enforcement institutions in Vietnam could join in December 2025 to exchange on internal controls, codes of conduct, and whistle-blower protection. • Non-state actors in anti-corruption in Malaysia
Jointly organized by UNODC, OHCHR, and SEA-CAN, could be convened in December 2025. Together with participants from CSOs, media, and youth groups, with opening remarks and participation of Swedish Ambassador Niklas Wiberg, they showcased innovative anti-corruption initiatives, including SEA-CANs open data project.
- Enhancing judicial integrity: the adoption of the Manila Statement on Judicial Integrity for South and Southeast Asia
A crucial result of the support for implementation of the Regional Roadmap on anti-corruption, human rights, and gender is the landmark adoption of the Manila Statement on Judicial Integrity for South and Southeast Asia on 21 November 2025 by Chief Justices, Justices, and senior members of the judiciary in the region. The Manila Statement demonstrates a shared commitment to judicial integrity and a foundation for future collaboration in i) Judicial independence; ii) Building trust and access to justice; iii) Responding to emerging threats against judicial integrity, such as corruption networks, political interference, and cybersecurity risks; iv) Harnessing digital transformation in the judiciary; v) Advancing open justice.
This is considered a key milestone in the regional anti-corruption networks in promoting judicial integrity. Co-organized by UNODC, OHCHR, and the Supreme Court of the Philippines, with co-funding with the Government of Sweden from the Danish International Development Agency and the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Korea, the high-level conference convened 21 Chief Justices, Deputy Chief Justices, and senior members of the judiciary from Bangladesh, Brunei Darussalam, Lao PDR, Indonesia, India, Maldives, Mongolia, the Philippines, and Thailand. This achievement was an direct outcome of the Regional Workshop on Judicial Security and Resilience held on 7 8 May 2026 in Manila.
- A key knowledge product as results of 2025 is regional report launched by UNODC and OHCHR in December on corruption and human rights, which analyzed the intersection of anti-corruption and human rights frameworks across ASEAN countries focusing on six thematic areas: i) Protection of whistle-blowers, witnesses, and human rights defenders; ii) Freedom of expression and the right to information; iii) Judicial integrity; iv) Business and human rights; v) Institutional frameworks and vi) Corruption and the death penalty.
